primitives.name: Touchback Condition
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is a Touchback when a player on defense permits a ball, kicked by an opponent, to strike his person and then roll across his goal line and he or any player of his side then falls on it back of the line.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'T': 'Boolean indicator for touchback event', 'B': 'Ball position vector (meters)', 'L_g': 'Goal line position vector (meters)', 'P_d': 'Defensive player position vector (meters)'}
primitives.assumptions: Ball trajectory is linear; player motion is negligible after impact; contact occurs at point of deflection.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When B · u_g < L_g · u_g and P_d · u_g > B · u_g where u_g is unit vector normal to goal line.

layer2.mapping: The touchback condition mirrors a boundary crossing event in stochastic processes, where a random walk crosses a threshold defined by the goal line.
layer2.telemetry: Ball position relative to goal line and player contact time

primitives.name: Not Touchback Juggle
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is not a Touchback if such player juggles the ball so that he in any way forces it over the line and he or any player of his side then falls on it.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'J': 'Boolean indicator for juggle event', 'F': 'Force vector applied by player (Newtons)', 'B': 'Ball position vector (meters)'}
primitives.assumptions: Player applies force directly to ball; ball does not roll naturally across line.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When F · ΔB > 0 and B · u_g < L_g · u_g but J = true.

layer2.mapping: Juggle introduces non-linear dynamics that alter ball trajectory, preventing standard boundary crossing logic.
layer2.telemetry: Force magnitude and direction during ball interaction

The touchback and safety rules define two distinct boundary-crossing scenarios in football. The touchback condition requires a defensive player to allow an opponent’s kick to strike them and roll across the goal line, followed by a fall behind the line. This implies a deterministic path of motion governed by Newtonian mechanics. In contrast, the not-touchback juggle rule excludes cases where a player forces the ball over the line, introducing a non-deterministic element via force application. The safety condition further complicates this by requiring the ball to be dead and the impetus to originate from the defending side. These conditions form a triadic logical structure: (1) boundary crossing (2) agent intent (3) causality chain. Each primitive operates within a phase space defined by ball position, player motion, and force vectors. The failure modes occur when these conditions are violated—e.g., if the ball rolls without contact or if impetus comes from the offensive side. Dualities emerge between the roles of offense and defense in determining outcome, with each rule defining a partition of possible game states.
